data.title: Per-row database read inside a loop (N+1)
data.description: A database **read** happens inside a loop body: N records means N round trips, which degrades into an N+1 query as the data grows. The fix is one batch fetch outside the loop (`findAllById(ids)` / `whereIn` / eager-loading the association) and pairing in memory. Two kinds of exceptions to exclude first: looping over a **constant-length** collection such as config or a dictionary (N is small, no change needed), and per-day / per-enum bucketed aggregation loops (N is bounded, an acceptable pattern).

params.label: Candidate call-site cap
params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases to speed up (at the cost of missing later call sites).

data.message: Per-row database read inside a loop ({name}) — N records = N queries; fetch in one batch outside the loop instead
data.remediation: Hoist the per-row query out of the loop into one batch fetch (findAllById / whereIn / eager-load the association), then pair by key in memory

data.title: Per-row database write inside a loop
data.description: A database **write** happens inside a loop body: N records means N INSERT / UPDATE round trips. Same root cause as the N+1 read, but a different fix — batch writes (`saveAll` / `insertBatch` / a single whereIn update) or merging several updates into one conditional update. Note: when the loop body carries business validation (each row must be checked individually before writing), per-row writes are **reasonable**; what should change then is the transaction boundary (wrap the whole thing in `@Transactional`), not forcing a batch.

params.label: Candidate call-site cap
params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases to speed up (at the cost of missing later call sites).

data.message: Per-row database write inside a loop ({name}) — N records = N writes; batch the writes or merge the updates into one
data.remediation: Switch to batch writes (saveAll / insertBatch / a single whereIn update); if each row needs its own validation, wrap the whole loop in one @Transactional instead

data.title: Hot table containing PII
data.description: Both a hotspot table and one holding personal information — blast radius and security sensitivity are both maxed out, so fix it first.

params.label: Fan-in threshold
params.description: A PII table must be referenced by >= this many places to be reported; lower it to catch sensitive-asset spread earlier.

data.message: Table {name} contains PII and is referenced by {param:min_fan_in} or more places; a sensitive asset with a large blast radius
data.remediation: Converge the access entries first and unify the masking egress

data.title: Event that is never triggered
data.description: An event node has no Triggers in-edge — declared but nobody dispatches it.
data.message: Event {name} has no trigger source (no Triggers in-edge)
data.remediation: Confirm whether the event is still used; if abandoned, delete the declaration

data.title: Queue that is never published to
data.description: A Queue / Topic node has no PublishesTo in-edge.
data.message: Queue {name} has no publisher (no PublishesTo in-edge)
data.remediation: Confirm whether the producer was removed, or extend FKB's publish verbs

data.title: Write endpoint has no auth capability recognised
data.description: An endpoint that changes state (POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE) has neither an Authentication capability annotation on the graph nor an explicit public-endpoint annotation. (Currently disabled: the Capability channel produces nothing yet, so the criterion does not hold.)
data.message: Write endpoint {name} has no auth capability recognised (it may genuinely have none, or the graph did not resolve the middleware)
data.remediation: Confirm whether this endpoint should require auth; if the middleware is within FKB's supported range but still unrecognised, add a capability rule

data.title: Write endpoint auth is optional (reachable without login)
data.description: The endpoint has an auth middleware attached, but the attached argument explicitly says optional (CRMEB's `AuthTokenMiddleware::class, false`): if you are logged in the identity is attached, if not you are let through anyway. "Optional" is not the same as "absent", so this is only reported when the graph actually saw that argument — if it did not see it, it stays silent (that is the graph failing to resolve, not the code failing to do it).
data.message: Write endpoint {name} has an auth middleware but the argument makes it optional (reachable without login) — confirm this is deliberate
data.remediation: If the endpoint must be logged in to operate (letting guests through while changing state is usually a vulnerability), change the attached argument to true; if the design really is "attach identity when logged in, still offer basic features when not", keep it.

data.title: Raw SQL execution site present
data.description: A call site marked as a sink by the Taint channel (whereRaw / query / execute / Db::raw …). Only the fact is reported; no judgement is made on whether the arguments come from the user.

params.label: Candidate call-site cap
params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases so one check does not get slow.

data.message: Raw SQL execution site {name} (at {file}:{line}) — confirm whether the arguments are parameterised
data.remediation: Switch to parameterised queries; if arguments come from user input this is an SQL injection risk

data.title: Table containing PII needs review
data.description: The table is annotated as containing personal information (phone number / national ID, etc.). The MVP only asks for a review; it does not judge whether encryption and masking are adequate. (Note: the `pii` annotation is produced by fkb/php/crmeb.yaml; other projects have no such annotation yet and will then be blocked by `rules_unavailable` rather than hard-reporting 0 hits.)
data.message: Table {name} was recognised as containing PII fields; confirm that encryption / masking / access auditing are in place
data.remediation: Check how the columns are stored and where they are exported; add a masking middleware if needed

data.title: User data concatenated into raw SQL (SQL injection)
data.description: A call site executes raw SQL (Db::query / Db::execute / Db::raw / whereRaw / whereExp) and a variable is concatenated directly into the SQL string (coming from a request or outside). Whether the variable is interpolated into the string or the whole SQL statement is passed in as a variable, both count as high-risk SQL injection. Judged by the P9 Taint phase.
data.message: The SQL at raw execution site {name} concatenates a variable directly (at {file}:{line}) — high-risk SQL injection
data.remediation: Switch to parameterised queries (? / :name placeholders, or ->where('col = ?', [$var])), never concatenate user input into an SQL string; if a table / column name must be concatenated, validate it against an allowlist.

data.title: User data concatenated into the where-condition string (SQL injection)
data.description: A variable is concatenated directly into the condition string of where / whereOr (e.g. ->where("CONCAT(',',roles,',') LIKE '%,$roles,%'")). This is SQL injection, fundamentally different from the parameterised form (placeholder + bound array). Judged by the P9 Taint phase.
data.message: where condition {name} concatenates a variable directly (at {file}:{line}) — SQL injection risk
data.remediation: Use the parameterised form ->where('col = ?', [$var]); never write a variable into the SQL string.

data.title: Raw SQL passed in as a variable, source to be confirmed
data.description: The call site executes raw SQL, but the variable concatenated into the SQL cannot be traced to a request source inside this function (often a function parameter, or assembled by logic outside this function and passed in). It may be a trusted source such as an upgrade script / config file, or an upstream caller may have brought request data in — this phase does no cross-procedure tracking and cannot decide at the call site, so it only hints and never blocks.
data.message: The SQL at raw execution site {name} comes from a variable (at {file}:{line}) — no request source visible inside this function; confirm whether upstream contains user input
data.remediation: If that SQL may ultimately contain user input, switch to parameterised queries; if it definitely comes from a script / config shipped with the package, disable this rule for the project (the rule-set page supports per-project overrides).

data.title: where condition passed in as a variable, source to be confirmed
data.description: The condition string of where / whereOr contains a variable, but no request source can be traced inside this function (typically a parameter, e.g. `$roles` in `searchRolesAttr($query, $roles)`). The only difference from `sql-injection-where-interp` is **evidence strength**: that one is proven to come from the request, this one needs a human to confirm the caller.
data.message: where condition {name} contains a variable (at {file}:{line}) — no request source visible inside this function; confirm whether the caller passes user input
data.remediation: Trace one level up to the caller; if it comes from the request, parameterise it; if it is an internal constant / config, disable this rule for the project.

data.title: CORS reflected origin (Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the request Origin)
data.description: The response header Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set directly to the request's Origin (or the whole Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is assembled from a variable). That treats requests from any site as same-origin and (often together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`) leaks user credentials — a high-risk CORS configuration. Judged by the P10 Cors phase.
data.message: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set to the request Origin (at {file}:{line}) — reflected origin, credential-level cross-origin leak
data.remediation: Use a fixed allowlist of origins, or do "compare against the allowlist and echo back" per request; never reflect request->header('origin') / $_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN'] back verbatim.

data.title: Signature compared with a loose operator (== / !=)
data.description: A signature value from an external callback is compared with `==` / `!=`. PHP's loose comparison makes digests of the `0e...` form judge each other equal (`md5('240610708') == md5('QNKCDZO')`), and the byte-by-byte early exit creates a timing side channel. Judged by the P11 Sign phase: a signature computation exists in the same function (md5 / sha1 / hash_hmac / *Sign()) and the signature value is compared loosely.

params.label: Candidate call-site cap
params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases so one check does not get slow.

data.message: The result of signature computation {name} is compared with == / != (at {file}:{line}) — loose comparison + non-constant time
data.remediation: Use hash_equals($expected, $actual) for a constant-time comparison; comparing as strings first introduces `0e...` type confusion and a timing side channel. Note: `===` / `!==` are strict but still not constant time, so hash_equals is recommended there too.

data.title: Signature uses md5 / sha1
data.description: A signature computation uses md5 or sha1. Most of the time the gateway officially requires it (MD5 signatures in WeChat Pay V2, the legacy Alipay API, some shipping / printing gateways), and then nothing needs to change; what deserves attention is a **self-built gateway** choosing a weak algorithm — that means the signature can be collided and forged.

params.label: Candidate call-site cap
params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases so one check does not get slow.

data.message: Signature uses the weak hash {name} (at {file}:{line}) — ignore if the gateway officially requires it; a self-built gateway should upgrade
data.remediation: Confirm the digest algorithm the gateway documentation requires; if it is self-built / optional, upgrade to HMAC-SHA256 or RSA-SHA256 and make sure the secret never takes part in plaintext concatenation.

params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases to speed up (at the cost of missing later call sites).

data.remediation: Hoist the per-row query out of the loop into one batch fetch (whereIn / eager-load the association), then pair by key in memory

data.message: Per-row database write inside a loop ({name}) — N records = N writes; batch the writes or merge the updates into one
data.remediation: Switch to batch writes (saveAll / insertAll / a single whereIn update); if each row needs its own validation, wrap the whole loop in one transaction

data.title: External system call inside a loop
data.description: A loop body calls an HTTP / SMS / email / RPC client (the list comes from FKB `external_calls`). One network round trip costs an order of magnitude more than one database query, and amplifying it N times serially is the classic cause of endpoint timeouts. Typical scenes: sending an SMS per user in a loop, querying shipping tracking in a loop, pulling remote images in a loop. Exception: when the loop is itself a "retry on failure / idempotent compensation" scenario (N is small and there is backoff), no change is needed.

params.label: Candidate call-site cap
params.description: Cap on the number of CallSite nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases so one check does not get slow.

data.message: External call {name} inside a loop (at {file}:{line}) — N records = N serial network round trips
data.remediation: Prefer a batch API from the third party (pass several ids at once); when no batch API exists, push the in-loop calls onto a queue for async processing, or at least issue them concurrently with a timeout — do not let N round trips block the request serially.

data.title: Multiple database writes with no transaction boundary recognised
data.description: One method writes directly to 2 or more different tables (the `WritesDb` edges left by P7 verb classification, excluding indirect edges propagated along the call chain), and the method has no transaction marker at all (`transaction` / `startTrans` / `commit` …). If any step in the middle fails, **partially successful** dirty data is left behind (the order was updated, the stock was not deducted). Two caveats: the transaction may be opened by an outer caller, which the graph cannot confirm across procedures; and `if/else` branches that each write the *same* table once **do not count** (mutually exclusive branches, so partial success is impossible).

params.label: Candidate method cap
params.description: Cap on the number of Method nodes checked; lower it on very large codebases so one check does not get slow.

data.message: Method {name} writes to the database several times but no transaction boundary was recognised (at {file}:{line}) — a partial failure leaves dirty data
data.remediation: Confirm whether these writes must be atomic: if so, wrap them in one transaction (and do not put remote calls inside it); if the transaction already lives further out, ignore this entry and bring the entry method into the recognised scope.

data.title: Event published but nobody listens
data.description: An EventBus node has Emits in-edges (publisher) but no ListensTo in-edge (listener). The typical cause is a refactor that removed the listener but left the emit line — this kind of code raises no error, it just **silently stops working**, often discovered months later.
data.message: Event {name} has a publisher but no listener on the graph — the broadcast is handled by nobody (or the listener registered under a dynamic name the graph could not resolve)
data.remediation: Confirm whether the listener still exists; if abandoned, delete the emit rather than keeping a broadcast nobody receives

data.title: Event listened to but never published
data.description: An EventBus node has ListensTo in-edges (listener) but no Emits in-edge (publisher). The listener therefore never fires — it is **dead code**, and deleting it changes no behaviour.
data.message: Event {name} has a listener but no publisher on the graph — the listener can never fire (or the publisher uses a dynamic name the graph could not resolve)
data.remediation: Confirm whether the publisher was deleted; if so, remove this listener (it can never execute)

data.title: Event bus with neither publisher nor listener
data.description: An EventBus node has neither Emits in-edges (publisher) nor ListensTo in-edges (listener). Unlike the other two "asymmetric" rules, this one is a **total orphan**: both ends are missing and the whole bus is isolated on the graph — usually leftover from a refactor, or both publishing and listening use dynamic names the graph could not resolve.
data.message: Event bus {name} has neither a publisher nor a listener — a total orphan on the graph (or dynamic names prevented resolution)
data.remediation: Confirm whether this event bus is still used; if abandoned, delete it entirely rather than keeping a bus with both ends empty

data.title: Hot table (high fan-in)
data.description: A table referenced by 50 or more places on the graph. It is usually a performance bottleneck and a coupling point that cannot be changed: touching one field means evaluating dozens of call sites. The threshold is tunable per project: a small database has a lower bar for "hot".

params.label: Fan-in threshold
params.description: Semantic in-edge count must be >= this value to report a hotspot; lower is more sensitive, higher reports only true central tables.

params.label: Candidate table cap
params.description: Cap on the number of table nodes checked, so a very large database cannot drag one check down.

data.message: Table {name} is a hotspot (semantic in-edges >= {param:min_fan_in}); consider caching / read-write splitting / sharding
data.remediation: Use the table perspective to see where the fan-in comes from and decide whether to converge the access entries

data.title: Config key read directly everywhere
data.description: A config key read directly by 50 or more places on the graph. This is not a bug, it is a **signal of change cost**: renaming the key means editing dozens or hundreds of call sites, and any one missed is only discovered at runtime.

params.label: Read-site threshold
params.description: The number of call sites reading the key must be >= this value; lower is more sensitive, higher shows only genuinely scattered keys.

data.message: Config item {name} is read directly by {param:min_reads} or more places (spread across many call sites), so renaming it means editing all of them
data.remediation: Converge on one config service / constant; business code should not read config keys directly all over the place

data.title: Table that is read but never written
data.description: The table is read (ReadsDb in-edges) but nothing on the graph writes it (no WritesDb in-edges). The application never writes it: the data may come from an external system / ETL / a seed script, or the write path uses a chain FKB did not recognise. Usually this is a legitimate read-only dimension table; the point is to "confirm who writes it".

params.label: Minimum read sites
params.description: The number of call sites reading the table must be >= this value; raise it to see only heavily-read read-only tables and filter out occasional queries.

data.message: Table {name} is read (>= {param:min_reads} places) but never written by the application — confirm the writer (external / ETL / seed) or an unrecognised write path
data.remediation: Confirm where the data comes from; if the write really happens inside the application, extend FKB's write-table verb recognition

data.title: High fan-out method (resource coupling hotspot)
data.description: A method's semantic fan-out (the number of tables / configs / caches it reads and writes directly) is very high. A method churning a large number of resources at once is usually a "god method": hard to test, hard to change, prone to regressions. The threshold is tunable per project: a small codebase has a lower bar.

params.label: Semantic fan-out threshold
params.description: The number of resources (table / config / cache) the method touches directly must be >= this value; raise it to report only genuinely out-of-control methods.

data.message: Method {name} reads and writes {param:min_fan_out} or more resources directly (semantic fan-out >= threshold); a high-coupling hotspot
data.remediation: See whether it can be split into several methods by responsibility; high fan-out usually means one method has swallowed several use cases

data.title: Contract declares a handler but it did not resolve to a method
data.description: The contract node carries a `handler` property (the route registration names a `controller/method` or a closure) but has no HandledBy out-edge — meaning **the route exists, the graph simply did not resolve it to a method node**. This is first of all a signal that "the graph is incomplete": no downstream conclusion built on it should be treated as final.

params.label: Only matching contracts
params.description: Substring filter on the name (case-insensitive). Empty = all contracts; fill in a prefix (e.g. /adminapi) to watch only one batch of routes, which narrows the scope a lot.

data.message: Contract {name} registers a handler but the graph did not resolve it to a method (no HandledBy out-edge) — the route is probably fine, the graph's resolution has a gap
data.remediation: Extend FKB's route-string / closure handler resolution rules; until then do not read this as "the endpoint is broken"

data.title: HTTP contract has no handler
data.description:
The contract node has no `handler` property at all and no HandledBy out-edge — its origin is unknown (auto-inferred route, a path assembled by the front end, or the other side never registered it at all). It may be a genuinely dead link or something the graph failed to recognise, so it is only a warning.
Only contracts **only the backend has ever synthesised** are considered (`side=backend`, i.e. `sides` holds a single party). Otherwise this rule and the "phantom call" one report the same batch of nodes twice (measured on p7/p8 where all 123 / 162 entries overlapped) — saying the same thing twice and doubling the warnings.

params.label: Only matching contracts
params.description: Substring filter on the name (case-insensitive); empty = all contracts.

data.message: Contract {name} has neither a handler property nor a HandledBy out-edge — possibly a real dead link, possibly an unrecognised route
data.remediation: Confirm whether the path really has a server-side implementation; for front-end callers also check the "phantom call" rule

data.title: Front end calls an endpoint that does not exist on the back end (phantom call)
data.description: The front end really calls the contract (a `CallsHttp` in-edge exists), but the contract has no HandledBy out-edge to a backend handler. The criterion is the **edge, not the `side` property**: several parties may write the same synthesised node, and the scalar `side` is only a derived label then (`bridge`), so "who knows about this node" belongs to the evidence, not to a property any party can overwrite. **Known limitation**: the baseURL prefix of front-end axios/request calls (e.g. `/adminapi/v1`) does not yet take part in identity normalisation, so many hits actually come from "the prefix was not joined" rather than a real phantom call — hence warning rather than error, and the wording spells out both possibilities.

params.label: Only matching contracts
params.description: Substring filter on the name (case-insensitive); empty = all front-end contracts.

data.message: The front end calls {name}, but the graph has no matching backend route (could be a real phantom call, or the front-end baseURL prefix was not normalised)
data.remediation: Sample and check by hand; if it is a prefix problem, add baseURL resolution rules to the front-end FKB

data.title: Backend endpoint has no caller (dead endpoint)
data.description: The backend has a handler, but nothing on the graph CallsHttp into it. Note that endpoints called by external systems / apps / third parties also match, so this is info level only.

params.label: Only matching endpoints
params.description: Substring filter on the name (case-insensitive); empty = all backend endpoints.

data.message: Endpoint {name} has a handler but no front-end caller at all; it may be a dead endpoint
data.remediation: Confirm whether a caller still exists (app / third party / scheduled task); if not, retire it

data.title: Table with no read or write reference at all
data.description: The table was created (SQL create table / Model `$table`) but has no read or write edge on the graph. Two possibilities: genuinely unused, or the graph is missing an edge.

params.label: Fan-in ceiling
params.description: Semantic in-edges must be <= this value to report; 0 = nobody references it at all, 1~2 tolerates a few references.

data.message: Table {name} has at most {param:max_fan_in} read/write reference(s) on the graph (possibly genuinely unused, possibly a missing edge)
data.remediation: Sample and confirm by hand; if code really does read and write it, FKB's read/write verb rules need extending

data.title: Table that is written but never read
data.description: The table has writes (WritesDb in-edges) but nothing on the graph reads it (no ReadsDb in-edges). Data written in is never read: either the expected shape for an audit / log table, or a defect — "writing to the wrong place" or "the read path was not recognised by FKB". The threshold is tunable per project, so you only watch tables that really are being written to.

params.label: Minimum write sites
params.description: The number of call sites writing the table must be >= this value; set it to 2~3 to see only tables that really are being written and filter out occasional single writes.

data.message: Table {name} is written (>= {param:min_writes} places) but never read — nobody uses the data written in; possibly a dead write path or an unrecognised read path
data.remediation: Confirm whether this is the expected shape for an audit / log table; otherwise check for a wrong target table, or code reading it that FKB did not recognise

data.title: GET endpoint performs a write
data.description: An HTTP contract whose name starts with GET but contains a write verb (delete / remove / destroy / truncate / insert / reset / purge / clear / wipe). REST semantics require GET to be read-only: a GET carrying a delete / clear action breaks cache and retry safety, and is easily triggered by crawlers or browser prefetch.

params.label: Only matching contracts
params.description: Substring filter on the name (case-insensitive); empty = all contracts.

data.message: Contract {name} is a GET but contains a write verb, violating REST read-only semantics (a retry or prefetch may trigger the write)
data.remediation: Change the endpoint to a write method such as POST / DELETE; if it really is a read-only clear / delete preview, rename it to avoid the write verb

data.title: Cache is read but nothing on the graph writes it
data.description: A Cache node has ReadsCache in-edges (some code reads it) but no WritesCache out-edges (nothing on the graph writes it). Two possibilities: reads always get empty / stale data (a real dead cache read), or the write path uses a mechanism the graph does not recognise (framework auto-caching, or another process filling it).

params.label: Only matching caches
params.description: Substring filter on the name (case-insensitive); empty = all caches.

data.message: Cache {name} is read but nothing on the graph writes it — reads may always be empty / stale, or the write path is unrecognised
data.remediation: Confirm the cache really has a writer; if a framework or another process fills it, add the corresponding write edge in FKB
